title: What is diabetes? Start with the basics
description: Understand what diabetes means, how the main types differ, and what a diagnosis can tell you.
sections: A problem with how the body uses energy

Diabetes is a condition in which the amount of glucose in your blood becomes too high. Glucose is a kind of sugar that your body uses for energy. You need it to think, move, work and get through your day. The problem is not having glucose. The problem is having more of it in the blood than your body can manage.

A hormone called insulin helps many of your cells take in glucose. When the body makes too little insulin, or has trouble using it, glucose can build up in the bloodstream. That is the basic idea behind diabetes, although different types develop for different reasons.
The main types are different

In type 1 diabetes, the immune system attacks the cells that make insulin. People with type 1 need insulin treatment. It can begin in childhood or adulthood, and it is not caused by eating too much sugar.

In type 2 diabetes, the body does not respond to insulin as well as it should, and over time it may not make enough. Family history, age, activity and other factors can influence risk. People of different body sizes can develop it. Gestational diabetes develops during pregnancy and needs its own care plan.
You cannot always feel it

Some people notice thirst, frequent trips to the bathroom, tiredness or blurry vision. Others feel completely normal, especially when type 2 diabetes develops gradually. Symptoms alone cannot tell you whether you have diabetes. Blood tests and a conversation with a healthcare professional are how you get a clearer answer.
Prediabetes is a related condition: blood glucose is above the usual range but below the range used to diagnose diabetes. It raises the risk of type 2 diabetes, but progression is not inevitable.
A diagnosis is a starting point

Diabetes care can include food choices, movement, medicines, monitoring and regular checkups. The details depend on the type of diabetes and the person. Taking medicine is a useful part of care when it is needed. It does not mean that someone has failed at changing their habits.

If you are newly diagnosed, start with three questions: What type do I have? What should I do first? When should we review my progress? You do not have to learn every term or change every routine in one afternoon.
Where UpNext fits

If you have prediabetes or an elevated risk of type 2 diabetes, explore UpNext’s Diabetes Prevention Program and its initial eligibility check. If you want to begin with everyday habits, Healthy Routines offers short lessons on eating, movement, sleep and stress. These learning programs support practical changes alongside appropriate healthcare.

title: What is glucose, and why does your body need it?
description: Glucose is fuel. Here is how food, your liver and insulin help your body use it.
sections: Glucose is a source of fuel

Glucose is a simple sugar that your body uses for energy. It travels through the blood so it can reach tissues around the body. Your brain and muscles need a steady supply of energy, whether you are reading a message, walking to the store or sleeping. Glucose is part of normal life, not something you need to remove from your body.

When people say blood sugar, they usually mean the glucose circulating in the blood. The word sugar can make this sound like it comes only from candy. It does not. Many everyday foods contribute to the glucose your body uses.
It comes from more than sweet foods

Your body breaks down many carbohydrates into sugars that it can absorb. Bread, rice, potatoes, fruit, milk and beans all contain carbohydrates. These foods differ in nutrients, fiber and portion size, so sharing one nutrient does not make them interchangeable.

A bowl of beans and a sugary drink can both affect blood glucose, but they offer very different things in a meal. Beans provide fiber and other nutrients. A sweet drink can supply a substantial amount of sugar without helping you feel as satisfied as a meal.
Your liver helps between meals

Food is not the only source. Your liver stores energy and can release or make glucose when you have not eaten for a while. This helps keep your body supplied overnight and between meals. That is one reason blood glucose is not determined only by the last thing you ate.

Insulin helps coordinate this system. After a meal, it helps many cells take in glucose and signals the body to store some energy for later. When this system is not working well, glucose may stay elevated in the blood.
A rise after eating is expected

Blood glucose normally changes during the day. A rise after a meal does not automatically mean diabetes, and you do not need to chase a perfectly flat line. What matters is the overall pattern, your health situation and, when appropriate, properly interpreted blood tests.

If you have diabetes, your care team may recommend a meter or sensor to understand your own pattern. If you do not, you can ask whether monitoring would actually help. A number without context can create confusion rather than answer a useful question.
Keep the focus on meals you can repeat

You do not have to memorize the chemistry of every food. A useful starting point is choosing regular meals with vegetables, a source of protein and carbohydrate foods that provide fiber. Your preferences, budget and any medical needs should shape the plan.

The everyday eating lessons in Healthy Routines help you think through small choices you can practice. Understanding glucose is a way to make food feel less mysterious, not a reason to be afraid of eating.

title: Blood glucose: what does that number mean?
description: Learn the difference between glucose and blood glucose, and why timing matters when you see a result.
sections: The fuel and the measurement

Glucose is the sugar your body uses for energy. Blood glucose describes how much of that sugar is in your blood at a particular time. If you have seen the word glycemia, it means the same general thing: the level of glucose in the blood. One word names the substance; the other describes its level.

In the United States, a glucose result is usually shown in milligrams per deciliter, written as mg/dL. Some countries use mmol/L. The numbers look different because the units are different, so always check the unit before comparing results.
Timing changes the meaning

A fasting blood glucose test is usually taken after at least eight hours without food or drinks other than water. A result taken after a meal reflects a different moment. An oral glucose tolerance test measures your response to a specific glucose drink. These tests cannot all be interpreted using one cutoff.

A home meter gives a reading for that moment. A continuous glucose monitor follows glucose in the fluid around cells and estimates its pattern over time. An A1C blood test gives a longer view. Each tool answers a slightly different question.
One reading is only part of the picture

Food, activity, illness, stress and medicines can affect blood glucose. Even the time of day can matter. If a result surprises you, start by asking how and when it was measured, whether you were fasting, and whether you were sick or taking a medicine that could influence it.

Home readings can help people manage diagnosed diabetes, but they are not a substitute for laboratory testing to establish a diagnosis. A healthcare professional may repeat a test or use another test to confirm what a result means.
A diagnosis and a daily goal are different

The cutoffs used to diagnose diabetes are not the same thing as the everyday targets given to someone already living with it. Daily targets may differ with age, pregnancy, medicines and other health conditions. Your friend's recommended range may not be right for you.

If you are monitoring at home, ask your care team what range to aim for, when to check, and what to do if a number is above or below that range. Write down the instructions so you are not trying to make a decision from memory.
Turn a number into a useful question

Instead of asking whether one number is good or bad, ask what it tells you and what happens next. Do you need another test? Is there a pattern worth reviewing? Would a small change to a meal or activity routine help? Those questions are more useful than judging yourself.

If testing shows prediabetes, UpNext’s Diabetes Prevention Program is one place to explore structured learning about lifestyle change. A test result should guide the next step, not define who you are.

title: Insulin and insulin resistance, in plain English
description: What insulin does, what resistance means, and why you can have insulin resistance without noticing it.
sections: Insulin helps the body use glucose

Insulin is a hormone made by the pancreas, an organ inside your abdomen. Hormones are chemical messages that help different parts of the body work together. One of insulin's jobs is to help many cells take in glucose from the blood and use it for energy.
A simple way to picture it is as a signal telling cells that fuel is available. The real process involves several steps, but you do not need to know all of them to understand why insulin matters.
Resistance means a weaker response

With insulin resistance, cells in muscles, fat and the liver do not respond to insulin as well as they should. The pancreas may compensate by making more insulin. For a time, that extra effort can keep blood glucose within the usual range.

If the pancreas can no longer keep up, blood glucose may rise. It can reach the prediabetes range and, in some people, the diabetes range. This is why insulin resistance and diabetes are related but are not identical. Having one does not automatically mean having the other.
There may be no obvious symptoms

People often cannot feel insulin resistance or prediabetes. You cannot reliably identify it from how tired you feel after lunch or how much you crave a snack. Those experiences have many possible explanations. A health professional can review your history and decide which tests make sense.

Routine testing often focuses on blood glucose and A1C rather than measuring insulin resistance directly. You do not need to order a long list of tests on your own to begin a useful conversation about risk.
Several factors influence risk

Family history, age, physical activity and body fat distribution can play a role. Conditions such as polycystic ovary syndrome can also be linked with insulin resistance. The combination differs from person to person. It is too simple to reduce the whole process to willpower or a single food.

Movement can help the body use glucose, and a sustainable eating pattern can support health. Weight loss may help some people with overweight or obesity, but the right goal depends on the person. Someone whose weight is already appropriate may need a different approach.
Choose a first step you can practice

You might begin with a short walk, a more regular meal routine, or replacing a sugary drink with water. These are possible starting points, not a personalized treatment plan. If you take glucose-lowering medicine, ask about any adjustments needed when changing activity or meals.

Healthy Routines offers short lessons to help turn an intention into something repeatable. If you have prediabetes, you can also explore the Diabetes Prevention Program. You can start learning without mastering every medical term.

title: Prediabetes: a chance to act early
description: What prediabetes means and how to turn a test result into a practical next step.
sections: Higher than usual, below the diabetes range

Prediabetes means your blood glucose is above the usual range but has not reached the range used to diagnose diabetes. It increases the chance of developing type 2 diabetes. It also deserves attention because it can travel alongside other risks to heart health.

The name can sound as though diabetes is already decided. It is not. Some people develop type 2 diabetes, others remain in the prediabetes range, and some return to lower glucose levels. Knowing about it gives you an opportunity to make a plan and follow up.
Feeling well does not rule it out

Prediabetes usually has no clear symptoms. You may feel fine and discover it during a routine blood test. That does not make the result meaningless. It means testing can reveal something that everyday feelings cannot.

A healthcare professional may use an A1C test, a fasting blood glucose test or another glucose test. Ask which test you had, what the result means, and when it should be checked again. Different tests provide different views of how your body handles glucose.
Small changes can have real value

Research on diabetes prevention found that a structured lifestyle program reduced the risk of type 2 diabetes in adults at high risk. The program combined changes to eating, physical activity and weight, with ongoing support. Its results do not promise the same outcome for every individual, but they show that prevention is more than wishful thinking.

For people with overweight, common prevention goals include losing about 5% to 7% of starting weight and building toward at least 150 minutes of moderate activity each week. These are goals to discuss and work toward gradually, not requirements you must meet immediately.
Your plan should fit your life

Begin by looking at what is realistic. Could you walk for ten minutes on three days this week? Would planning one easy lunch make afternoons simpler? Is there a drink you could change without feeling deprived? Pick an action that you can identify clearly and repeat.

Ask your clinician about other parts of the plan, including blood pressure, cholesterol and whether medication would be helpful in your circumstances. Lifestyle changes and medical care can work together. There is no need to treat them as competing choices.
Get support for the part that is hard

UpNext’s Diabetes Prevention Program includes an initial eligibility check and a year-long learning experience focused on practical habits. Explore the program information to understand its format and whether it fits your needs.
If you prefer to begin with shorter everyday lessons, Healthy Routines covers eating, movement, sleep and stress. The most useful first step is one you can continue, then review as your needs change.

title: What is A1C? The blood test with a longer view
description: A simple guide to A1C, common result ranges, and the questions to ask about your test.
sections: A view of the past few months

A1C is a blood test that helps show your average blood glucose over roughly the past three months. You may also hear it called HbA1c or hemoglobin A1C. It gives a longer view than a glucose reading taken at one moment, although recent weeks influence the result more than earlier weeks.

Glucose attaches to hemoglobin, a protein inside red blood cells. The A1C test measures the share of that protein with glucose attached. You do not need to remember the chemistry. The useful idea is that A1C helps reveal a pattern rather than one morning's reading.
The common ranges

For diagnosing diabetes in people who are not pregnant, an A1C below 5.7% is generally below the prediabetes range. A result from 5.7% to 6.4% falls in the prediabetes range. A result of 6.5% or higher falls in the diabetes range.

These are diagnostic ranges, not personal grades. If you have no clear symptoms, a result in the diabetes range generally needs confirmation with repeat testing. Pregnancy and some other health situations require different testing decisions, so your clinician should interpret the result with you.
A1C has limits

An average cannot show every high and low during the day. Two people can have a similar A1C and quite different glucose patterns. Someone taking insulin may therefore use home readings or a sensor alongside A1C to make day-to-day decisions.

Some types of anemia, hemoglobin variants and other conditions can make A1C less reliable. Recent blood loss or a transfusion can also affect it. Tell your healthcare professional about these circumstances, especially if the result does not seem to match your other glucose readings.
You usually do not need to fast

An A1C test itself usually does not require fasting. However, if your appointment includes other blood tests, the instructions may be different. Check with the clinic or laboratory rather than assuming that every test in the same appointment has the same preparation.

After the result, ask whether you need another test and when to repeat A1C. The interval depends on whether the test is for screening, confirming a diagnosis or monitoring diabetes treatment. There is no single schedule that fits everyone.
Ask what the result changes

Useful questions include: Does this suggest prediabetes or diabetes? Could anything make my A1C inaccurate? What should I do next? If I already have diabetes, what target is appropriate for me? A diagnosis threshold and a treatment target serve different purposes.

If your result points to prediabetes, you can explore UpNext’s Diabetes Prevention Program while arranging medical follow-up. The number is a piece of information you can use to choose a next step. It does not tell the whole story of your health.

title: Diabetes symptoms: what should you pay attention to?
description: Recognize common signs, understand why diabetes can be silent, and know when to seek urgent help.
sections: Some changes are worth checking

Feeling thirstier than usual, urinating more often, unexplained tiredness and blurry vision can be symptoms of diabetes. Frequent infections or wounds that heal slowly can also be reasons to contact a healthcare professional. These symptoms can have other causes, so noticing them is a reason to ask questions rather than diagnose yourself.

A useful detail is whether something has changed from your usual pattern. Are you getting up several times at night to urinate? Is your thirst unusual even when you drink normally? Write down when the change started and whether other symptoms appeared with it.
Weight loss can be a warning sign

Losing weight without trying, particularly alongside thirst, frequent urination or unusual hunger, deserves medical attention. When the body cannot use glucose properly because there is too little effective insulin, it may begin breaking down other energy stores.

This is different from gradual, planned weight loss as part of an appropriate health plan. Do not assume an unexplained drop on the scale is automatically a healthy change. Tell a clinician, including how much weight changed and over what period.
Diabetes can also be quiet

Type 2 diabetes may develop slowly, and some people notice few or no symptoms. Prediabetes is often silent too. Waiting until you feel sick can therefore miss an opportunity for earlier care. Testing may be appropriate because of your health history even if you feel well.

Type 1 diabetes symptoms often appear more quickly, although adults can have a slower onset. It can begin at any age. A person's age or body size cannot reliably tell you which type of diabetes they have.
Know when help is urgent

Vomiting, abdominal pain, trouble breathing, fruity-smelling breath, fainting or marked confusion can signal a serious emergency, including diabetic ketoacidosis. Seek emergency medical care if these occur, especially with thirst, frequent urination or known diabetes. You do not need to wait for a routine appointment or a home test before getting help.

For less urgent symptoms, contact your healthcare provider promptly and ask whether you should be tested. A blood test and medical assessment can help separate diabetes from other possible explanations.
Bring a short, clear description

You can say: I have been much thirstier for two weeks and I am waking up to urinate more often. That gives the clinician more useful information than saying you think your sugar is off. Mention medicines, recent illness and any family history of diabetes.

UpNext’s Healthy Routines can help you learn about everyday health habits, but symptoms need assessment before you choose a learning program as your next step. If testing later shows prediabetes, the Diabetes Prevention Program may be relevant. Start with understanding what is happening.

title: Weight loss and diabetes: what is the connection?
description: Why weight can affect diabetes risk, when weight loss can help, and why the scale is only one measure.
sections: Weight is part of the picture

Body fat, especially around the abdomen, can influence how well the body responds to insulin. For some people with overweight or obesity, losing a modest amount of weight can help improve blood glucose and lower the risk of type 2 diabetes. That does not mean weight explains every case.

People at different weights develop diabetes. Family history, age, medicines and other health factors also matter. A number on a scale cannot tell you whether someone has diabetes or how much effort they are putting into their health.
What a modest change means

For adults with overweight who are at high risk of type 2 diabetes, prevention guidance often uses a goal of losing about 5% to 7% of starting weight. For someone weighing 200 pounds, that is about 10 to 14 pounds. It is a modest change relative to starting weight, not a demand to reach a particular appearance.

The major prevention research combined weight loss with physical activity, changes to eating and structured support. Weight was one part of a broader program. The benefit should not be treated as a promise that a particular number of pounds will guarantee a particular result.
Healthy change takes more than restriction

Planned weight loss usually involves changing the balance between energy taken in and energy used over time. But the way you do that matters. A plan should provide enough nutrition and be realistic to continue. Skipping meals or cutting out many foods can be difficult to maintain and may create risks with some diabetes medicines.

A clinician or registered dietitian can help decide whether weight loss is appropriate and how to approach it. Medicines or other treatments may be options for some people. Needing additional support does not mean that everyday habits are useless.
Look beyond the scale

Walking more comfortably, preparing meals more regularly and improving a blood test can all be meaningful progress. Changes in body weight can also reflect water and other factors, so a short-term rise or fall does not tell you exactly how body fat has changed.

Unplanned weight loss is a different situation. If you lose weight without trying, especially with thirst or frequent urination, contact a healthcare professional. It can be a symptom of diabetes or another condition that needs attention.
Choose support that matches your goal

UpNext’s Diabetes Prevention Program focuses on practical changes for people who may be at risk of type 2 diabetes. Start with its eligibility information and discuss your health goals with your clinician.

Healthy Routines offers shorter lessons on everyday eating, movement, sleep and stress. If weight loss is not appropriate for you, there are still habits worth building. The goal is better health with a routine you can live with.

title: Eating for blood glucose without making food complicated
description: A practical starting point for meals, carbohydrates, portions and foods you already enjoy.
sections: Start with a meal, not a forbidden list

Eating for blood glucose does not require finding one perfect food. The overall pattern matters: what you eat, how much, when you eat and how the meal fits your medicines and activity. Your plan should also fit your culture, budget and the foods you can actually get.

If you have diabetes, a registered dietitian or diabetes educator can help adapt meals to your needs. General ideas are a starting point. They cannot tell you exactly how many carbohydrates to eat or whether a change is safe with your medicine.
Carbohydrates are not all the same

Rice, bread, fruit, beans, potatoes and milk contain carbohydrates that can affect blood glucose. They also differ in fiber, protein, vitamins and other nutrients. It makes more sense to consider the whole food and its portion than to treat every carbohydrate as something to avoid.

Whole grains, beans and whole fruit can be part of a healthy eating pattern. Portion size still matters. A large serving of a nutritious food may affect your glucose differently from a smaller serving, especially when you are managing diabetes.
Try the plate method

One simple approach uses a plate about nine inches across. Fill roughly half with nonstarchy vegetables such as leafy greens, broccoli or peppers. Use about a quarter for protein such as fish, chicken, eggs or tofu, and about a quarter for carbohydrate foods such as rice, potatoes or beans.

This is a flexible guide rather than a rule for every dish. A soup, sandwich or mixed meal can contain the same parts in a different arrangement. Beans provide both carbohydrate and protein, so you can adjust the rest of the meal accordingly.
Drinks and routines count too

Water and unsweetened drinks are practical everyday choices. Juice and sweetened drinks can add a lot of carbohydrate without the fiber found in whole fruit. Changing one regular drink may be an easier first step than redesigning every meal.

Meal timing can matter if you use insulin or certain other diabetes medicines. Skipping or delaying food can increase the risk of low blood glucose. Ask your care team before making major changes, and do not stop or adjust medicines on your own.
Make the next meal easier

Choose one action for the week: keep frozen vegetables available, plan a simple lunch, or prepare one protein you can use in several meals. Notice what makes the action easy or difficult, then adjust. A meal plan that only works on your least busy day needs more flexibility.

The everyday eating lessons in Healthy Routines can help you practice small changes. For people at risk of type 2 diabetes, the Diabetes Prevention Program puts eating into a broader habit-building process. Begin with a change you can repeat.

title: How movement helps your blood glucose
description: Why activity matters and how to build a routine without starting with an intense workout.
sections: Your muscles use fuel when you move

Walking, dancing, swimming and other activities make your muscles use energy. Physical activity can help the body use glucose and respond better to insulin. It can also support heart health, strength and everyday functioning. You do not need to begin with a gym membership to get moving.

Movement is useful even when the scale does not change. Weight is one possible measure of progress, but it is not the only reason to be active. Feeling stronger or finding a routine you enjoy can make it easier to continue.
Build toward a weekly pattern

A common goal for adults is at least 150 minutes of moderate activity each week. Moderate activity makes your heart beat faster and your breathing a little harder. During a brisk walk, you can usually talk but would find singing difficult.

That weekly goal can be broken into smaller sessions. If you are starting from very little activity, a short session is a reasonable beginning. Ten minutes after lunch on a few days can be more manageable than promising yourself an hour every morning.
Choose something that fits your body

A walk is one option, not the only option. Seated exercise, wheelchair rolling, water-based movement and adapted activities can also help people be active. Your abilities, health conditions and preferences should shape what you choose.

Strength activities are also valuable. Many adults aim to work major muscle groups at least twice a week, using weights, resistance bands or appropriate body-weight exercises. Start at a level that feels manageable and ask for guidance if pain, balance or other limitations make it difficult.
Diabetes medicines can change the plan

If you take insulin or medicines that can cause low blood glucose, activity can lower glucose during or after a session. Ask your care team whether you should monitor it, carry a fast-acting carbohydrate or follow particular instructions. Do not make medicine changes based on general exercise advice.

Health problems affecting your feet, eyes or heart may also change which activities are appropriate. If you have very high glucose or have been told to check for ketones, follow your clinician's plan. Exercise is not a replacement for treating a glucose emergency.
Give the habit a clear place

A useful plan names the activity, time and frequency: I will walk for ten minutes after lunch on Monday, Wednesday and Friday. Then decide what you will do if it rains or your day runs late. A smaller alternative can help you keep the routine going.

Healthy Routines includes lessons on movement and building habits. UpNext’s Diabetes Prevention Program connects activity with other practical changes for people at risk of type 2 diabetes. Pick a starting point that works for your body and your week.
